title: Quick to check. Quick to find?
hook: Checking a sum takes one addition. How much work is finding one?

knows: the number of choices multiplies fast (route-explosion)
doesNotKnow: that checking a proposed answer can take one step while finding one, or proving none exists, can mean trying every group, and that this gap is the P versus NP question

misconception: If checking an answer is quick, finding an answer must be about as quick.
objective: The learner can explain that checking 4 + 5 = 9 takes one addition, while finding a group of the six numbers that makes 9 took 21 tries and proving none makes 13 took all 64, that each extra number doubles the groups, and that whether a fast general finding method exists is the P versus NP question.

claims.text: Six numbers form 2^6 = 64 groups (each number in or out, including the empty group); seven numbers form 128, so one more number doubles the groups (readout 'Groups: each number in or out 2⁶ = 64').
claims.source: Each number is in or out of a group independently: 2^n groups. 2^6 = 64, 2^7 = 128.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14): stage readout now states the reason (learner r10); previously verified by fact-checker on 2026-10-14. Earlier note: Derivation: each number in or out, 2^n groups; 2^6 = 64, 2^7 = 128. The stage grid is 2^nums.length squares. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Re-derived in python: 2^6 = 64 groups (each number in or out, empty group included), 2^7 = 128. The new readout label 'Groups: each number in or out' with value 2⁶ = 64 (2⁷ with the 7th number) states exactly this.

claims.text: Trying the groups of 3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2 one by one in binary counting order (number b in the group when bit b of the group number is set, list order, starting with the empty group), the first group that sums to 9 is the 21st tried, {4, 5}; no group sums to 13, so the one-by-one search tries all 64. (A shortcut exists for this list: 34 and 12 cannot be in a group making 13.)
claims.source: search() in src/demos/cs/checking-is-not-finding/model.ts; builder's node enumeration 2026-10-14: first sum 9 at index 20 (21st tried) = {4, 5}; groups summing to 9: {4, 5} and {3, 4, 2}; groups summing to 13: 0. The fact-checker can redo it by listing the 64 sums.
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14): question and status now say the search is one by one (learner r10: this list has shortcuts); previously verified by fact-checker on 2026-10-14. Earlier note: Re-ran search() and an independent enumeration of all 64 sums: first sum 9 at index 20 (21st tried) = {4, 5}; groups with sum 9: {4,5} and {3,4,2}; no group sums to 13 (13 is not among the 64 sums), so 64 tried. The reveal's hard-coded '21st' matches FIND9.tried = 21. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Own enumeration of the 64 groups of [3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2] in binary counting order: first sum 9 at index 20 (21st tried) = {4, 5}; groups summing to 9: {4, 5}, {3, 4, 2}; 13 is not among the 64 sums, so a one-by-one search tries all 64. The parenthetical shortcut holds: 34 > 13, and 12 + the smallest other number (2) = 14 > 13, so neither can be in a 13. The new question and status text ('one by one') match.

claims.text: Checking the proposed group 4 + 5 = 9 takes one addition (checking any group takes one addition per extra number in it).
claims.source: A group of k numbers needs k - 1 additions to total; {4, 5} needs 1.
claims.note: Derivation: a group of k numbers needs k - 1 additions; {4, 5} needs 1.

claims.text: A shortcut can help on one list, but for problems like this, called NP problems, a proposed answer is quick to check, yet nobody knows a method that finds one quickly in every case; whether such a method exists is the P versus NP question.
claims.source: CLRS 3e ch. 34 (NP as problems verifiable in polynomial time; section 34.5.5: subset-sum is NP-complete); Karp (1972), 'Reducibility among combinatorial problems'. Caveat kept in the wording: a table method is fast when the numbers are small (pseudo-polynomial), so the reveal says 'nobody knows', never 'impossible' or 'always exponential'. Attribution: fact-checker confirms. | v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, W-686): reworded from 'always finds one without a search that grows this fast', which meet-in-the-middle (2^(n/2) + 2^(n/2) sums, about 1.41x per number) makes false. 'Quickly' means in time polynomial in the input size. Still needs an openable source for subset-sum NP-completeness (CLRS 34.5.5 / Karp 1972 were not opened).
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (W-839, 2026-10-14): reveal adds 'A shortcut can help on one list' (learner r10); previously verified by fact-checker on 2026-10-14. Earlier note: Pass 37 (W-732): verified on an opened source in place of the unopened CLRS 34.5.5 / Karp 1972: Boaz Barak, Introduction to Theoretical Computer Science (git clone github.com/boazbk/tcs, commit 68d6dde, 2026-10-06). lec_13_Cook_Levin.md: NP = problems whose solutions can be efficiently verified (definition NP-def, line 64; fig. line 62), and the Cook-Levin theorem that 3SAT is NP-complete (line 241). lec_12_NP.md line 346: theorem 'Hardness of subset sum', 3SAT <=p SSUM, with the input length counted in bits (line 343), which matches the reveal's 'nobody knows' and the pseudo-polynomial caveat. SSUM is in NP (the group is the certificate; checking it is one sum), so it is NP-complete. lec_14_PvsNP.md line 29: whether P = NP (equivalently a polynomial-time algorithm for 3SAT) is 'the great open question'; line 228: 'we don't know efficient algorithms for NP complete problems'. The new wording no longer claims a 2x-per-number search is forced, so the meet-in-the-middle objection is closed. Builder (non-blocking): add the Barak citation to the source field and drop the unopened CLRS/Karp, or mark them unopened. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. The new clause 'A shortcut can help on one list' is shown on this list (c2: 34 and 12 cannot be in a 13) and does not contradict 'nobody knows a method that finds one quickly in every case'. recall.question: Someone hands you a filled-in Sudoku and says it is solved. Compared with solving a blank one yourself, checking their grid is usually:
recall.why: Checking a proposed answer takes one pass over it; finding one can mean searching a number of possibilities that multiplies with every blank. That gap between checking and finding is what P versus NP asks about.
